synopsis: Mixed motion requires predicting both participants’ future positions, with collision decisions based on the machine’s predicted swept volume and the other actor’s trajectory rather than proximity or object labels alone [f14031, f14034, f7021, f7476]. Straight-line time to collision is insufficient for sideways, rotating or initially stationary motion, and turning, articulation or skid steering can create collisions without longitudinal closing speed [f14039, f5920, f13731]. Motion scope must be defined machine by machine: ISO 21815-3:2023 covers forward/reverse intervention, Part 4 excludes automatic braking during rotation, and draft Part 5 reached proof stage on 9 September 2026 for other motion forms [f10906, f10900, f10902, f10904]. Pretoria’s October 2024 steering-rate collision-prediction results were simulation-only; production recommendations treat steering as an avoidance cue, not proof of safety, and require demonstrably safer predicted trajectories before suppressing intervention [f6331, f6367, f6336, f6342]. Recorded replay cannot establish other actors’ reactions after counterfactual braking, so closed-loop simulation needs regenerated observations and reactive agents, while mixed motion also requires controlled whole-machine tests because validated off-road behavioral models were not found [f5525, f14043, f5539, f14041, f14042]. Planning remains constrained by missing accident speed/motion detail and worldwide motion-type collision shares, and the proposed single swept-volume collision logic must be reconciled with concerns about treating swing and rotation as one function [f3256, f3610, f7021, f10899].

relations.note: Both identify differential speed, skid turning and counter-rotation as collision-relevant motions.
